facts.statement: Manidens is the sister taxon of the closely related South African dinosaur Pegomastax.
facts.quote: It is a sister taxon of the closely related Pegomastax from South Africa.

facts.statement: The type species Manidens condorensis was described in the journal Naturwissenschaften in 2011.
facts.quote: The type species of Manidens, Manidens condorensis, was described in the journal Naturwissenschaften in 2011.

facts.statement: Manidens was named by Diego Pol, Oliver Rauhut, and Marcos Becerra.
facts.quote: Manidens was named in by Diego Pol, Oliver Rauhut and Marcos Becerra.

facts.statement: The generic name Manidens refers to the hand-shaped form of its posterior lower teeth.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Latin manus, "hand", and dens, "tooth", a reference to the hand-shaped form of the posterior lower teeth.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MPEF-PV 3211 consists of a partial skeleton including a skull, lower jaw, axial column, left shoulder girdle, and pelvis.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Manidens, MPEF-PV 3211, consists of a partial skeleton with a skull and lower jaw, including the axial column except most of the tail; a left shoulder girdle; and the pelvis.

facts.statement: Manidens had high-crowned teeth adapted for a herbivorous diet but lacked the wear facets found in more advanced forms.
facts.quote: It has high-crowned teeth indicative of an increased adaptation to a herbivorous diet but lacks the wear facets seen in more advanced forms like Heterodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Manidens may have possessed filamentous integumentary structures based on evidence from the related Tianyulong.
facts.quote: The discovery of filamentous integumentary structures in the related Tianyulong suggests that they may also have been present in other heterodontosaurids such as Manidens.

facts.statement: Manidens exhibited asynchronous tooth replacement in a continuous anterior-to-posterior wave pattern.
facts.quote: Tooth replacement was asynchronous in Manidens, which exhibited dental replacement in a continuous anterior-to-posterior wave pattern.

facts.statement: Manidens is the first known heterodontosaurid to show dental replacement in its caniniform teeth, which may have occurred at a different time than its cheek teeth.
facts.quote: Furthermore, Manidens represents the first known occurrence of a heterodontosaurid with dental replacement of its caniniform teeth, which may have had distinct timing relative to its cheek dentition.

facts.statement: Fossils of Manidens were found in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in Chubut Province, Argentina, and are dated to the Toarcian stage.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in Chubut Province, Argentina, considered to be originally dated to the Bajocian, latter were found to be from Toarcian beds.

facts.statement: Manidens lived approximately 179 to 178 million years ago during the Middle-Late Toarcian.
facts.quote: The specimens were found in the Queso Rallado locality of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, dating originally to the Aalenian–Early Bathonian stages, 171 ± 5 to 167 ± 4 Ma, yet where latter constrained to 179-178 million years, that is Middle-Late Toarcian.

facts.statement: Manidens had a sacrum made of six fully fused vertebrae supported by robust ribs and ossified tendons that likely stiffened its back.
facts.quote: The sacrum consists of six fully fused vertebrae, with extensive fusion of centra, zygapophyses, and most neural spines, supported by robust sacral ribs that anchor to the ilium; ossified tendons are present along the sacral region, likely providing dorsal stiffening.

facts.statement: Manidens possessed distinctive proatlases in its neck vertebrae, a feature first reported in heterodontosaurids that connected to the skull base.
facts.quote: Cervical vertebrae are relatively short with robust processes for rib attachment, including distinctive proatlases (first reported in heterodontosaurids) that articulate with the skull base.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Manidens include a probable toe bone from the fourth digit and a flattened wrist bone.
facts.quote: Scattered appendicular remains include a probable pedal phalanx from the fourth digit and a flattened proximal carpal bone.

facts.statement: Manidens was a relatively basal heterodontosaurid that grew up to 60 to 75 centimeters long, making it smaller than later forms.
facts.quote: Manidens era un heterodontosáurido relativamente basal que llegaba hasta los 60 a 75 centímetros de largo, lo que lo hace menor que heterodontosáuridos posteriores.

facts.statement: Manidens had high-crowned teeth indicating an adaptation to a herbivorous diet, though they lacked the worn facets seen in advanced forms like Heterodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Sus dientes de coronas altas son una indicación de un incremento en la adaptación a la dieta herbívora pero carecen de las facetas desgastadas vistas en formas más avanzadas como Heterodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Filamentous integumentary structures found in the relative Tianyulong suggest that Manidens may also have possessed them.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento de estructuras filamentosas integumentarias en Tianyulong, un pariente cercano sugiere que también pueden haber estado presentes en otros heterodontosáuridos como Manidens.

facts.statement: Manidens had long toe bones capable of grasping, with a smaller hallux that could still grip, similar to tree-perching birds.
facts.quote: The long toe bones indicate that the toe bones were capable of grasping; distinct anchor attachments for the muscles and tendons of the hallux indicate that its hallux was smaller than the rest of the toes but could still have grasped.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Manidens may have been at least partially arboreal.
facts.quote: Fossils attributed to Manidens from Argentina indicate that this dinosaur may have been at least partially arboreal.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that Manidens may have been partially carnivorous based on its unusual tooth morphology.
facts.quote: Based on the unusual morphology of its teeth, it has been speculated that Manidens may have been partially carnivorous, as has occasionally been suggested for heterodontosaurids.

facts.statement: Manidens lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately 171 to 167 million years ago, in what is now South America.
facts.quote: Manidens condorensis es la única especie conocida del género extinto Manidens de dinosaurio ornitisquio heterodontosáurido que vivió a mediados del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente entre 171 a 167 millones de años durante el Bajociano en lo que es hoy Sudamérica.

facts.statement: Manidens fossils were found in the Queso Rallado locality of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, dating to the Aalenian or early Bathonian, 171 ± 5 to 167 ± 4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Los especímenes fueron encontrados en la localidad de Queso Rallado de la formación Cañadón Asfalto, datando del Aaleniense o principios del Bathoniense, 171 ± 5 to 167 ± 4 millones de años.

facts.statement: The genus Manidens existed from the Toarcian to the Aalenian, between 184.2 and 170.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Toarcian to Aalenian (184.2 to 170.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Manidens fossils come from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, an environment with lacustrine and fluvial deposits that coevolved with volcanic activity.
facts.quote: The holotype of Manidens comes from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation. This member is mostly made of two major depositional settings: lacustrine and fluvial deposits, that have intervals of tuffaceous materials, suggesting this environments coevolved with volcanic activity.

facts.statement: Manidens condorensis was described in 2011 by Diego Pol, Oliver Rauhut, and Marcos Becerra.
facts.quote: La especie tipo de Manidens, Manidens condorensis, fue descrita en la publicación Naturwissenschaften en el año 2011. Manidens fue nombrado por Diego Pol, Oliver Rauhut y Marcos Becerra.

facts.statement: The generic name Manidens comes from Latin for "hand" and "tooth", referring to the open-hand shape of the lower teeth at the back of the jaw.
facts.quote: Su nombre genérico se debe al latín manus, "mano", y dens, "diente", lo cual se refiere a la forma de mano abierta de los dientes inferiores en la parte posterior de la mandíbula.

facts.statement: The specific name condorensis refers to the Cerro Cóndor town near the Queso Rallado site where the specimen was found by zoologist Guillermo Rougier.
facts.quote: El nombre específico se refiere al pueblo de Cerro Cóndor, localizado cerca del sitio Queso Rallado donde el espécimen fue hallado por el zoólogo Guillermo Rougier.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MPEF-PV 3211 consists of a partial skeleton with a skull, lower jaw, most of the axial column, the left shoulder girdle, and the pelvis.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo de Manidens, MPEF-PV 3211, consiste de un esqueleto parcial con cráneo y la mandíbula inferior, incluyendo la columna axial exceptuando la mayor parte de la cola; la parte izquierda de la faja de los hombros y la pelvis.

facts.statement: Manidens is classified in the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Heterodontosauridae

facts.statement: Manidens is the sister taxon to a clade containing the African species Heterodontosaurus, Abrictosaurus, and Lycorhinus, indicating an early evolutionary radiation of heterodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Manidens es el taxón hermano de un clado consistente de las especies africanas Heterodontosaurus, Abrictosaurus y Lycorhinus, indicando una temprana radiación evolutiva de los heterodontosáuridos.

facts.statement: Pol et al. regard the genus Echinodon as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: *Note: Pol et al. regard Echinodon as a genus of Heterodontosauridae.
